subject: physics

items.q: The specification defines momentum by an equation. Which word equation is that definition?
items.correct: momentum = mass × velocity
items.misconception: momentum = mass × acceleration
items.why: Both equations begin with mass and are taught within days of each other, so the second quantity is mixed up. Check what the second quantity is: velocity gives momentum in kg m/s, acceleration gives force in newtons.
items.random_wrong: momentum = weight × velocity

items.q: Which symbol equation for momentum does the specification give?
items.correct: p = m v
items.misconception: p = m × a
items.why: Both equations begin with mass and are taught within days of each other, so the second quantity is mixed up. Check what the second quantity is: velocity gives momentum in kg m/s, acceleration gives force in newtons.
items.random_wrong: p = ½ m v²

items.q: Which unit does the specification give for momentum, p?
items.correct: kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
items.misconception: newtons per second squared, N/s²
items.why: Momentum is first met alongside forces and crashes, and students associate the push of a collision with the newton. Build the unit from the equation: kg for mass multiplied by m/s for velocity gives kg m/s.
items.random_wrong: kilogram per metre second, kg/m s

items.q: A ball has a mass of 400 g and travels at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
items.correct: 2 kg m/s
items.misconception: 80 kg m/s
items.why: The equation is met as a multiplication and is practised that way, so the operation is remembered rather than the rearrangement. Decide which symbol is unknown first, rearrange p = m v for that symbol, and only then substitute.
items.random_wrong: 0.4 kg m/s

items.q: A lorry's speed is given as 54 km/h. What must be done before this value is used in p = m v?
items.correct: It must be converted to metres per second, by dividing by 3.6, because v in p = m v is in m/s
items.misconception: It can be put straight into p = m v as 54, because km/h is already a unit of speed
items.why: km/h is the unit students see on road signs and in car adverts, so it feels like the natural unit of speed. Check the unit of every quantity first. Velocity must be in m/s, so divide a speed in km/h by 3.6.
items.random_wrong: It can be substituted just as it is, provided the mass of the lorry is given in kilograms

items.q: A skateboarder of mass 60 kg moves at 4 m/s. What is the skateboarder's momentum?
items.correct: 240 kg m/s
items.misconception: 15 kg m/s
items.why: The equation is met as a multiplication and is practised that way, so the operation is remembered rather than the rearrangement. Decide which symbol is unknown first, rearrange p = m v for that symbol, and only then substitute.
items.random_wrong: 0.067 kg m/s

items.q: A 40 000 kg lorry moves at 3 m/s. A 1200 kg car moves at 30 m/s. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The lorry has the greater momentum: 120 000 kg m/s against only 36 000 kg m/s for the car
items.misconception: The car has the greater momentum, because it is the faster moving of the two vehicles
items.why: In everyday speech 'momentum' means something like unstoppable speed, and the first examples students meet vary the speed while leaving mass unmentioned. Calculate both. Multiply mass by velocity for each object and compare the two numbers.
items.random_wrong: They have equal momentum, since the lorry's extra mass is cancelled by the car's extra speed

items.q: A trolley of mass 5 kg has a momentum of 12 kg m/s. What is its velocity?
items.misconception: 60 m/s
items.why: The equation is met as a multiplication and is practised that way, so the operation is remembered rather than the rearrangement. Decide which symbol is unknown first, rearrange p = m v for that symbol, and only then substitute.

items.q: Why is the unit of momentum kilograms metre per second?
items.correct: Because momentum is mass × velocity, so the unit must be kg multiplied by m/s, or kg m/s
items.misconception: Because it is the unit of force multiplied by the unit of the time for which that force acts
items.why: Momentum is first met alongside forces and crashes, and students associate the push of a collision with the newton. Build the unit from the equation: kg for mass multiplied by m/s for velocity gives kg m/s.
items.random_wrong: Because momentum is mass × acceleration, so the unit is kg multiplied by m/s² instead

items.q: The specification states conservation of momentum for a closed system. What is a closed system?
items.correct: One in which no mass enters or leaves and no resultant force acts on it from outside the system
items.misconception: One in which the objects are all sealed inside a container, so that nothing can escape from it
items.why: The everyday sense of 'closed' is a shut box, so the condition is read as a physical enclosure rather than as a condition on mass and force. Ask instead whether anything outside the chosen objects is pushing on them or adding mass to them.
items.random_wrong: One in which nothing is moving, so that the total momentum of the system stays equal to zero

items.q: In a closed system the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. What is this called?
items.correct: Conservation of momentum
items.misconception: Conservation of net force
items.why: Both equations begin with mass and are taught within days of each other, so the second quantity is mixed up. Check what the second quantity is: velocity gives momentum in kg m/s, acceleration gives force in newtons.
items.random_wrong: Newton's third law of motion

items.q: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. Which statement about their momentum is correct?
items.correct: They have equal and opposite momenta, so the total is still zero, as it was before the push
items.misconception: Both of the skaters are now moving, so the system has gained momentum from the push they gave
items.why: Motion is equated with momentum, and the direction of the two velocities is not taken into account. Before the push the total is zero, so the total afterwards is also zero: the two momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction.
items.random_wrong: Each skater simply keeps the momentum it began with, which was zero for both

items.q: A moving trolley collides with a stationary trolley and slows down, while the second trolley moves off. Which description is correct?
items.correct: The momentum lost by the first trolley equals the momentum gained by the second, so the total is unchanged
items.misconception: Some momentum was destroyed in the collision, which is why the first trolley slowed down
items.why: The car visibly stops and nothing else appears to move, so momentum seems to vanish rather than transfer. Identify the whole closed system first. Momentum is transferred to whatever exerted the force, even if that object is far too massive for its motion to be seen.
items.random_wrong: Each trolley keeps the momentum it began with, since momentum is a conserved quantity

items.q: (physics only) A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley. They stick together. What is their velocity after the collision?
items.misconception: 4 m/s
items.why: The first trolley is the one 'doing' the moving, so the second is treated as being carried along rather than as part of the mass. When objects stick together they move as one object: add the masses before dividing the total momentum by them.
items.random_wrong: 12 kg m/s

items.q: (physics only) A 0.5 kg ball moving at 8 m/s hits a stationary 1.5 kg ball. The first ball stops. What is the velocity of the second ball?
items.misconception: 12 m/s
items.why: The equation is met as a multiplication and is practised that way, so the operation is remembered rather than the rearrangement. Decide which symbol is unknown first, rearrange p = m v for that symbol, and only then substitute.
items.random_wrong: 8 m/s

items.q: (physics only) A 50 kg skater at rest pushes a 15 kg sledge away at 4 m/s. What is the skater's velocity after the push?
items.correct: 1.2 m/s backwards
items.misconception: 4 m/s backwards
items.why: Newton's third law gives equal forces, and equal forces are assumed to produce equal speeds whatever the masses are. Set the two momenta equal: m₁v₁ = m₂v₂. The larger mass then has the smaller velocity.
items.random_wrong: 13.3 m/s backwards

items.q: (physics only) A resultant force acts on an object that is free to move. What does the specification say happens?
items.correct: A change in momentum occurs, because the force changes the object's velocity in that time
items.misconception: The object's momentum is transferred into the force, which is why the object slows down again
items.why: The car visibly stops and nothing else appears to move, so momentum seems to vanish rather than transfer. Identify the whole closed system first. Momentum is transferred to whatever exerted the force, even if that object is far too massive for its motion to be seen.
items.random_wrong: The mass of the object changes, since momentum is mass × velocity and the momentum changes

items.q: (physics only) Which two equations does the specification combine to give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)?
items.correct: F = m × a and a = (v - u)/(t)
items.misconception: p = m a and a = (v - u)/(t)
items.why: Both equations begin with mass and are taught within days of each other, so the second quantity is mixed up. Check what the second quantity is: velocity gives momentum in kg m/s, acceleration gives force in newtons.
items.random_wrong: F = m × a and a = ∆v × ∆t

items.q: (physics only) Which statement describes the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) correctly?
items.correct: The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, divided by the time taken for that change
items.misconception: The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, multiplied by the time over which it changes
items.why: Students read the equation as a product rather than a quotient, and 'more time' is assumed to mean 'more of everything'. ∆t is on the bottom of the fraction, so increasing it decreases the force.
items.random_wrong: The force equals the time taken divided by the change in momentum that occurs during it

items.q: (physics only) In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆ v represent?
items.correct: The change in momentum, that is the mass multiplied by the change in velocity
items.misconception: The force acting on the object, because force equals the change in momentum
items.why: 'Rate of change' is a compound phrase and the 'rate of' part is dropped, especially as both are described in terms of the same crash. 'Rate of' always means 'per second'. A change of 300 kg m/s in 0.1 s is a force of 3000 N; the same change in 1 s is 300 N.
items.random_wrong: The total momentum the object had before the force began to act on it, in kg m/s

items.q: (physics only) The specification says force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of' add?
items.correct: That the change in momentum is divided by the time taken for that change to happen
items.misconception: Nothing of substance; the force is simply equal to the change in momentum that takes place
items.why: 'Rate of change' is a compound phrase and the 'rate of' part is dropped, especially as both are described in terms of the same crash. 'Rate of' always means 'per second'. A change of 300 kg m/s in 0.1 s is a force of 3000 N; the same change in 1 s is 300 N.
items.random_wrong: That the momentum is multiplied by the time for which the resultant force acts on the object

items.q: (physics only) Why does an air bag reduce the force on a passenger during a crash?
items.correct: It increases the time taken for the change in momentum, lowering the rate of change
items.misconception: It reduces the passenger's change in momentum, so there is less momentum to be got rid of
items.why: 'Reducing the impact' is heard as reducing everything about it, and the change in momentum is confused with the force. The change in momentum is fixed by the mass and the change in velocity. The safety feature lengthens the time, which lowers the rate of change of momentum and so the force.
items.random_wrong: It absorbs most of the force of the crash, so that only a little of it reaches the passenger

items.q: (physics only) A gymnast lands on a crash mat rather than on the bare floor. Why is the force on the gymnast smaller?
items.correct: The mat squashes, so the momentum falls to zero over a longer time, making F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) less
items.misconception: The mat soaks up much of the force of the landing, so that only a small share of it reaches the gymnast
items.why: 'Absorbing the impact' is an everyday phrase, and force is imagined as a substance that can be soaked up. Force is not a stored substance. The mat increases the time for the same change in momentum, and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) then gives a smaller force.
items.random_wrong: The mat reduces the gymnast's momentum before the landing, so there is less momentum to be removed

items.q: (physics only) A 70 kg passenger moving at 12 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s without an air bag, and in 0.6 s with one. What are the two forces?
items.misconception: 84 N and 504 N
items.why: Students read the equation as a product rather than a quotient, and 'more time' is assumed to mean 'more of everything'. ∆t is on the bottom of the fraction, so increasing it decreases the force.
items.random_wrong: 8400 N and 504 N

items.q: An 8000 kg lorry crawls at 2 m/s; a 1000 kg car does 20 m/s. Which has the greater momentum?
items.correct: The car: 1000 × 20 = 20 000 kg m/s, against 8000 × 2 = 16 000 kg m/s for the lorry.
items.misconception: The heavier object always has the greater momentum, because momentum is about how massive something is.
items.why: Mass is the first quantity in the equation and the most striking feature of a lorry, so students compare masses and stop before finishing the multiplication. Neither quantity decides alone. Work out mass × velocity for both objects before comparing.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is kg m/s² an acceptable way to write the unit of momentum?
items.correct: No. kg m/s² is the newton, the unit of force; momentum is in kg m/s.
items.misconception: The unit of momentum has a squared second in it, like the unit of acceleration.
items.why: Students carry the s² across from acceleration and from F = m × a, where kg m/s² really is the correct combination. Only the units of the quantities in the equation appear: momentum is mass × velocity, so kg × m/s = kg m/s.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A ball has a mass of 400 g and moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
items.correct: 2 kg m/s, because 400 g must first be converted to 0.4 kg.
items.misconception: Momentum is 2000 kg m/s: substitute the mass as it is given, 400 × 5.
items.why: The number in the question looks ready to use, and the unit kg m/s is not read as an instruction about the mass. Convert to SI units before substituting: divide a mass in grams by 1000 to get kilograms.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two trolleys of equal mass approach each other at the same speed. What is the total momentum?
items.correct: Zero, because they move in opposite directions, so their momenta have opposite signs and cancel.
items.misconception: The total is found by adding the two momenta as plain numbers, giving double the momentum of one trolley.
items.why: Momentum is introduced through a multiplication, so it is treated like mass or energy, a quantity with size but no direction. Choose one direction as positive and give any momentum in the other direction a negative sign before adding.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A moving trolley hits a stationary one and slows down. Has momentum been conserved?
items.correct: Yes. The momentum lost by the first trolley has been gained by the second, so the total is unchanged.
items.misconception: Conservation of momentum means every object keeps the momentum it started with.
items.why: The word 'conserved' suggests nothing changes anywhere, so it is applied to each object instead of to the system total. Conservation applies to the total for the closed system: add up all the momenta before and after and compare those totals.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is momentum the same thing as kinetic energy?
items.correct: No. Momentum is m v; kinetic energy is a different quantity, calculated differently.
items.misconception: Momentum is the same quantity as kinetic energy: it is worked out with the energy formula ½ m v², so its equation is the energy equation.
items.why: Both quantities involve mass and speed and are met in the same topic, so the two formulae become blurred. Momentum uses velocity once, with no half and no square: p = m v, in kg m/s.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a seat belt reduce the force on a passenger?
items.correct: By stretching slightly, so the passenger is brought to rest over a longer time.
items.misconception: A seat belt works by stopping the passenger more quickly, before they can hit anything.
items.why: Seat belts are described as holding you firmly in place, which sounds like stopping you sooner rather than later. A shorter stopping time gives a larger rate of change of momentum and a larger force. The belt must extend the time, not cut it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should the weight of a car be used in p = m v?
items.correct: No. The equation needs the mass in kilograms, not the weight in newtons.
items.misconception: Weight and mass are the same 'how heavy' quantity, so either can be substituted.
items.why: In everyday use 'weight' is quoted in kilograms, which hides the distinction the physics makes. Weight is a force in newtons; mass is in kilograms. Only the mass belongs in p = m v.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A trolley's momentum changes from 12 kg m/s to 4 kg m/s. What is the change in momentum?
items.correct: A decrease of 8 kg m/s: final minus initial, 4 - 12 = -8 kg m/s.
items.misconception: The change is 16 kg m/s, found by adding the two momenta together.
items.why: Students add the numbers in the question rather than subtracting, especially when both are described as momenta of the same trolley. Change means final value minus initial value: subtract, and take the direction into account if the object rebounds.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a collision the total momentum is 12 kg m/s and the moving mass afterwards is 5 kg. What is the velocity?
items.correct: 2.4 m/s: the total momentum must still be divided by the mass that is moving.
items.misconception: The total momentum is the answer, so the velocity after the collision is 12.
items.why: Conservation of momentum gives a number that feels like the final answer, and the last step of dividing by the mass is dropped. Conservation gives the momentum after the event, not the velocity. Divide that momentum by the mass that is moving.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.7 Momentum (HT only)
